1.definition: The pre-Islamic religious system of Arabia, in which individual tribes each venerated their own patron deities — typically associated with sacred stones, trees, springs, or celestial bodies. No unified pantheon or organized priesthood existed across the peninsula. Mecca's Kaaba served as a deliberately pluralistic sanctuary housing roughly 360 idols, allowing tribes with different gods to coexist at the shared pilgrimage site. The Prophet Muhammad's monotheism directly challenged this arrangement by requiring exclusive worship of a single God.

2.definition: The earliest biography of the Prophet Muhammad, compiled around 770 CE by Ibn Ishaq (and preserved in a later edition by Ibn Hisham, around 830 CE). The title means 'Life of the Messenger of God.' It is the foundational narrative source for Muhammad's life and the early Muslim community, covering his birth, the first revelations, the Hijra, the battles of Badr and Uhud, the conquest of Mecca, and his death in 632 — though it was composed 100 to 200 years after the events it describes.

Muhammad's Arabic nickname before his prophetic career, meaning 'the trustworthy' or 'the faithful.' The epithet reflected his reputation in Mecca for reliability and honesty in commercial dealings. Islamic tradition treats it as evidence of his character before the revelations began; modern scholars note it appears in sources written centuries after his death.

The full Arabic name for Medina, meaning 'City of the Prophet.' After Muhammad's migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622, the oasis town of Yathrib was renamed Madinat al-Nabi, usually shortened in English to Medina. The city became the first Islamic political community and the headquarters of the early Muslim state under Muhammad and the four Rashidun caliphs.

3.definition: Describing communities who used Greek as their primary language of administration, liturgy, and daily life — including the late Roman bureaucracy the Umayyads inherited in Syria and Egypt, and the urban Christian populations of former Byzantine cities. Greek had been the common language of the eastern Mediterranean since Alexander's conquests and remained the working tongue of the Byzantine state until the Arab conquest shifted administration to Arabic.

The full Arabic title taken by Abu Bakr on becoming the first caliph, meaning 'Successor of the Messenger of God.' The Arabic word khalifa — 'successor' or 'deputy' — is the source of the English word 'caliph.' The title defined the new role as political continuation of Muhammad's leadership rather than a new prophetic office; Abu Bakr explicitly rejected any claim to prophethood.

The Byzantine Armenian general who commanded the Byzantine forces at the Battle of Yarmouk in 636 CE. Vahan had earlier served as governor of Syria under Emperor Heraclius. His defeat by the Arab Muslim army under Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah was the decisive battle that ended Byzantine rule in Syria and the Levant.

4.definition: Modern country in the Levant, between Syria and the Mediterranean; during the Umayyad period its territory was administered as part of the province of Syria (Bilad al-Sham). The modern state emerged under French mandate after World War I.

The period of Byzantine iconoclasm (726–842 CE), when emperors Leo III and his successors banned the veneration of religious images, triggering decades of theological conflict between Constantinople, Rome, and the Eastern churches. The controversy shaped Byzantine religious culture and relations with the papacy.

A branch of early Christianity (the Church of the East) that rejected the 431 CE Council of Ephesus, holding that Christ's divine and human natures were fully distinct. Nestorian Christians spread eastward through Persia and Central Asia; they are mentioned in the Umayyad cross-civ context as one of Christianity's major denominational schisms, parallel to the Sunni-Shia split in Islam.

The eighteen-year-old son of Husayn ibn Ali, killed at Karbala in 680 while defending his father. He is venerated in Shia tradition as a young martyr; his death is a recurring theme in the Ashura mourning rituals.

A nephew of Husayn ibn Ali (son of Husayn's brother Hasan), killed as a youth at Karbala in 680. His death, like those of Husayn's other young relatives, became a focus of the Shia commemorative tradition that grew up around the massacre.

5.definition: Describing communities who used Greek as their primary language of administration, liturgy, and daily life — including the late Roman bureaucracy the Umayyads inherited in Syria and Egypt, and the urban Christian populations of former Byzantine cities. Greek had been the common language of the eastern Mediterranean since Alexander's conquests and remained the working tongue of the Byzantine state until the Arab conquest shifted administration to Arabic.

The naval force built by the Umayyad governor Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan in the 640s–650s using Egyptian and Syrian shipwrights and Coptic crews. Mu'awiya's fleet defeated the Byzantine navy at the Battle of the Masts in 655, making the eastern Mediterranean an Arab-contested sea for the first time and enabling later campaigns including the Siege of Constantinople (717–718).

6.definition: The Pannonian Basin — the broad, flat lowland of central Europe (in modern-day Hungary and surrounding regions) that lies north of the Balkans. In the eighth century the region was contested steppe territory not yet settled by Hungarians (who arrived in 895); the term here is a geographic retronym for the corridor that would have opened to Arab armies had Constantinople fallen in 718.

The Arabic name for the Central Asian region beyond the Oxus River (Amu Darya), meaning 'That Which Lies Beyond the River' — the area of modern Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and southern Kazakhstan. The region's major cities, Bukhara and Samarkand, had been Sogdian Iranian-language trading centers for over a millennium before the Arab conquest under Qutayba ibn Muslim (709–715). The name emphasizes the geographic perspective of the Arab conquerors: this was the territory across the frontier river.

7.definition: The Arabic concept of divine decree or predestination — God's foreknowledge and determination of all that will happen. In early Islamic theology, the Qadariyya debated whether humans have genuine free will to act morally or whether everything is determined by divine decree. The Umayyad establishment favored strong predestinarianism, since it implied that whatever the caliphs did was God's will; the Qadariyya position that humans are responsible for their choices was seen as politically subversive.

The theological principle of 'deferral' — the Murji'a school's doctrine that judgment about whether a Muslim who commits a major sin is still a Muslim should be deferred to God rather than decided by the human community. The position was politically convenient for the Umayyad caliphate, since it implied that even caliphs who committed atrocities (like the killing of Husayn at Karbala or the bombardment of Mecca) retained their religious legitimacy, as no human had the authority to exclude them from the Muslim community.

Modern country in the Levant; in the Umayyad period its territory was administered as part of the province of Syria (Bilad al-Sham). The Umayyad desert palace of Anjar was built in present-day Lebanon.

A branch of early Christianity (the Church of the East) that rejected the 431 CE Council of Ephesus's definition of Mary as 'God-bearer,' holding that Christ's divine and human natures were distinct. Spreading eastward through Persia and Central Asia, Nestorian missionaries reached Tang China — the Xi'an Stele (781 CE) records their presence in the capital.
The Christian European armies who seized Jerusalem in 1099 and held it on and off until the late 1200s, briefly turning the Dome of the Rock into a church before Saladin's forces retook the city.

8.definition: One of the two great rival Arab tribal confederations that divided the Umayyad military and administration. The Qaysi (also called northern or Mudar Arabs) traced their ancestry to north Arabian tribes and competed bitterly with the Kalbi/Yamani (southern Arab) faction for provincial governorships, military commands, and caliphal favor. The tribal feud, rooted in pre-Islamic rivalries, continued inside the Umayyad state and became a major structural weakness — different caliphs backed different factions, and by the 740s the feuding had severely degraded the army's coherence.

The inhabitants of Khorasan — the eastern Iranian province that stretched from modern northeastern Iran into parts of Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. Under the Umayyads, Khorasan had a mixed population of Arab settlers, Persian-speaking Iranians, and Central Asian mawali converts. The Khorasanis were the primary military base of the Abbasid Revolution: Abu Muslim recruited among Arab garrison settlers, Persian-speaking mawali, and disaffected Yamani tribal clans to build the army that overthrew the Umayyad dynasty.

The village near Merv in Khorasan where Abu Muslim raised the Abbasid black banner in June 747, formally beginning the revolt against the Umayyad Caliphate. The site, in modern Turkmenistan, is the geographic starting point of the Abbasid Revolution — the moment when the underground Abbasid network went public with an armed uprising.

The 756 battle outside Córdoba in which Abd al-Rahman I defeated the Abbasid-appointed governor of al-Andalus, Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Fihri, and established his independent Emirate of Córdoba. The battle secured the Umayyad survivor's control of the Iberian Peninsula and created a separate Umayyad state in the west that would last nearly three centuries, eventually declaring itself a rival caliphate in 929.

The small Egyptian village where the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II was cornered and killed in August 750 by Abbasid forces pursuing him across Syria and into Egypt. His death, six months after the decisive Battle of the Zab, ended the Umayyad dynasty as a ruling power in the east.
